content: During pregnancy, a woman who is Rhesus-negative (Rh-negative) may develop antibodies if her fetus is Rhesus-positive (Rh-positive). This immune response can lead to complications such as fetal morbidity or mortality in subsequent pregnancies if left untreated. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of administering anti-D immunoglobulin (Ig) to Rh-negative women without pre-existing anti-D antibodies following a spontaneous miscarriage. The researchers conducted a search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to December 31, 2012. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the administration of anti-D Ig after spontaneous miscarriage to either no treatment or a placebo. Two reviewers independently assessed the trials for inclusion and quality, and they extracted and verified the data. Only one RCT met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 48 women who experienced a miscarriage between 8 and 24 weeks of gestation. In the treatment group, 19 women received a 300 µg intramuscular injection of anti-D Ig. Of these, 14 underwent therapeutic dilatation and curettage (D&C), while 5 had spontaneous miscarriages. In the control group, 29 women received a placebo injection of 1 cc homogenous gamma globulin. Among them, 25 underwent therapeutic D&C, and 4 had spontaneous miscarriages. The primary outcomes of interest—development of a positive Kleihauer-Betke test (a test used to detect fetal cells in maternal blood) and the occurrence of RhD alloimmunisation in subsequent pregnancies—were not reported in the included study. Similarly, none of the secondary outcomes were reported. These secondary outcomes included the need for increased fetal surveillance, fetal blood sampling, or fetal transfusions in subsequent pregnancies; neonatal complications such as anemia, jaundice, bilirubin encephalopathy, erythroblastosis, prematurity, or hypoglycemia; and maternal adverse events related to anti-D administration, such as anaphylactic reactions or blood-borne infections. The study did report subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies in three women from the treatment group and six women from the control group. However, due to the small sample size, the study was unable to demonstrate any significant difference in maternal sensitization or the development of Rh alloimmunisation in subsequent pregnancies. In conclusion, the available data are insufficient to evaluate the effectiveness of administering anti-D immunoglobulin to unsensitized Rh-negative women after a spontaneous miscarriage. Until high-quality evidence becomes available, the decision to use anti-D prophylaxis in this context should be guided by the standard practice guidelines of individual countries.
